summary: The Dhammapada is a collection of short verses, grouped into chapters on themes such as thought, earnestness, anger, the fool, the wise, the self and thirst. Each verse puts one point plainly: the mind shapes what we are, hatred is not ended by hatred, taming oneself is the hardest victory, and craving drives suffering. The verses are sayings attributed to the Buddha, and they point toward the eightfold path and Nirvana. This edition is F. Max Muller's English translation from the Pali.
context: Tradition says the Buddha spoke each verse on a particular occasion, and the commentary attributed to Buddhaghosa, in the fourth or fifth century CE, supplies stories to go with them. The text sits in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali Canon, and similar collections survive in Gandhari, Sanskrit, Tibetan and Chinese. European scholars took it up in the nineteenth century: Fausboll edited the Pali in 1855, and Max Muller made the first complete English translation in 1870. The site carries that translation, as it appears at Project Gutenberg.

ideas.title: Mind makes what we are
ideas.note: The opening verses say our experience follows our thoughts, as a wheel follows the ox's foot.

ideas.title: Earnestness against heedlessness
ideas.note: The earnest do not die, while the thoughtless are as if dead already.

ideas.title: Overcome anger by love
ideas.note: A man should beat anger with love and evil with good.

ideas.title: Craving causes suffering
ideas.note: The chapter on thirst compares craving to a creeper that grows and to water that falls off a lotus leaf once overcome.

ideas.title: Training the self
ideas.note: Taming oneself is called better than taming elephants or horses.

passages.quote: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts
passages.why: The first verse, on thought and suffering.

passages.quote: Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death
As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back
passages.why: The unsteady mind compared to an arrow.

passages.quote: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter
passages.why: The ground of the rule against killing.

passages.quote: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth
The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see
Mules are good, if tamed, and noble Sindhu horses, and elephants with large tusks; but he who tames himself is better still
The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest
